power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P = 0.23 ", Sentence = "No individual estimate reached nominal significance (minimum P = 0.23 across the 32 tests among GWAS passing heritability QC; minimum Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.95)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 15 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  0 of 914 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 914 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (15 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``chr`, `pos_hg19``, ``rsID``, ``ref`, `alt`` while the data has `Genetic_ID`, `Specimen_ID`, `Date_mean`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 29 codebook/README/label sources and 914 data columns across 84 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (15 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``chr`, `pos_hg19``, ``rsID``, ``ref`, `alt`` while the data has `Genetic_ID`, `Specimen_ID`, `Date_mean`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

- **Duplicated column names in `Vernot_et_al_2016_introgressed_variants_hg19.txt`.** 1 column name appears more than once (worst: `T`×2), so 2 of the file's 6 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 224 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (224). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 914 columns across 84 data files.
#### Issues Identified

32 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 84 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 20 scripts: 2 ran without error, 16 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts need a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: condition_locus.R, examine_locus.R. Naming the file in the script solves this. **3 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `compare_refits.R` (locus_summary.txt); `select_fits.R` (locus_summary.txt); `update_locus_overrides.R` (fine_mapping_loci.txt). Then this one ran to the end: `update_locus_overrides.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **3 scripts looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data.zip/neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data/fine_mapping/locus_summary.txt` to `data/fine_mapping/locus_summary.txt` for `refit_nonconverged.R`; `neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data.zip/neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data/fine_mapping/fine_mapping_loci.txt` to `data/fine_mapping/fine_mapping_loci.txt` for `regenerate_plink_for_figures.R`; `neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data.zip/neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data/introgressed_variants/merged_introgressed_variants_hg19.txt` to `data/introgressed_variants/merged_introgressed_variants_hg19.txt` for `regenerate_plink_for_figures.R`; `neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data.zip/neanderthal_ancestry_and_cancer_risk_data/fine_mapping/credible_set_summary.txt` to `data/fine_mapping/credible_set_summary.txt` for `update_locus_overrides.R`. **`setwd()` in the code**
**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

> INTROGRESSED_FILE <- file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "data/introgressed_variants/merged_introgressed_variants_hg19.txt")
> PALINDROMIC_PAIRS <- c("AT", "TA", "CG", "GC")
> load_gwas_config <- function(config_key, metadata_yaml = METADATA_YAML, quiet = FALSE) {
>   metadata <- yaml::read_yaml(metadata_yaml)
>   config <- metadata[[config_key]]
>   if (is.null(config)) stop(glue("Key '{config_key}' not found in {metadata_yaml}."))
> 
>   # LD panel and introgression maps are hg19, so use the lifted-over sumstats when the GWAS is hg38.
>   # positions_build records which build the positions in config$input are on.
>   config$positions_build <- if (is.null(config$assembly)) NA_character_ else config$assembly
>   if (identical(config$assembly, "hg38")) {
>     hg19_path <- file.path(dirname(config$input), paste0(config_key, "_hg19.txt.gz"))
>     if (file.exists(hg19_path)) {
>       if (!quiet) message(glue("Assembly is hg38. Switching input to hg19 file: {hg19_path}"))
>       config$input <- hg19_path
>       config$positions_build <- "hg19"
>     } else {
>       warning(glue("hg38 detected but {hg19_path} not found. Proceeding with original (hg38) input."))
>     }
>   }
>   config
> }
> load_sumstats <- function(config) {
>   source_cols <- c(config$rsID_column, config$chr_column, config$pos_column,
>                    config$effect_allele_column, config$other_allele_column,
>                    "beta", "standard_error")
>   std_cols <- c("rsID", "chr", "pos", "gwas_ea", "gwas_oa", "beta", "se")
> 
>   # a sentinel such as "." in a numeric column makes fread type the whole column as
>   # character, which fails later at beta / se rather than here
>   sumstats <- fread(config$input, select = source_cols,
>                     na.strings = c("NA", "na", ".", ""),
>                     colClasses = list(character = c(config$effect_allele_column, config$other_allele_column)))
>   setnames(sumstats, old = source_cols, new = std_cols)
> 
>   for (column in c("pos", "beta", "se")) {
>     if (!is.numeric(sumstats[[column]])) {
>       coerced <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sumstats[[column]]))
>       n_unreadable <- sum(is.na(coerced) & !is.na(sumstats[[column]]))
>       message(glue("{column}: {n_unreadable} values could not be read as a number; set to NA."))
>       sumstats[, (column) := coerced]
>     }
>   }
> 
>   # Same cleaning as the Neanderthal list so exact matching is fair
>   sumstats[, rsID := normalize_rsids(rsID)]
>   sumstats
> }
> extract_window <- function(sumstats, lead_rsid, window_size, drop_variants = NULL) {
>   if (!(lead_rsid %in% sumstats$rsID)) {
>     stop(glue("Lead rsID {lead_rsid} not found in summary statistics."))
>   }
> 
>   lead <- sumstats[rsID == lead_rsid][1]
>   half_window_bp <- (window_size * 1000) / 2
>   window_start <- lead$pos - half_window_bp
>   window_end   <- lead$pos + half_window_bp
> 
>   in_window <- sumstats[chr == lead$chr & pos >= window_start & pos <= window_end]
>   in_window <- in_window[!is.na(rsID) & rsID != "."]
>   in_window <- in_window[!duplicated(rsID)]
>   in_window <- in_window[!is.na(se) & se > 0]
> 
>   if (!is.null(drop_variants)) {
>     message(glue("Manually removing {length(drop_variants)} requested variants from the window..."))
>     in_window <- in_window[!(rsID %in% drop_variants)]
>   }
> 
>   list(variants = in_window,
>        chr = gsub("chr", "", as.character(lead$chr)),
>        start = window_start,
>        end = window_end)
> }
> normalize_rsids <- function(ids) {
>   ids <- trimws(as.character(ids))
>   ids <- sub("^RS", "rs", ids)
>   sub("^(rs[0-9]+):.*$", "\\1", ids)                # rs123:A:G -> rs123
> }
> load_introgressed_variants <- function(path = INTROGRESSED_FILE) {
>   intro <- fread(path, sep = "\t", colClasses = list(character = c(
>     "chr", "rsID", "ref", "alt", "alleles", "neanderthal_allele", "maps", "notes")))
>   intro[, rsID := normalize_rsids(rsID)]
>   intro[, pos_key := paste0(chr, "_", pos_hg19)]
>   message(glue("Loaded {nrow(intro)} introgressed variants from {path} ",
>                "({intro[is.na(rsID), .N]} without rsID; {intro[!is.na(neanderthal_allele), .N]} with a Neanderthal allele)"))
>   intro
> }
> allele_pair <- function(a, b) {
>   a <- toupper(a); b <- toupper(b)
>   fifelse(is.na(a) | is.na(b), NA_character_, paste(pmin(a, b), pmax(a, b), sep = "/"))
> }
> match_introgressed <- function(rsID, chr, pos, a1, a2, intro, use_position = TRUE) {
>   a1 <- toupper(a1); a2 <- toupper(a2)
>   idx <- match(rsID, intro$rsID, incomparables = NA)
>   if (use_position) {
>     need <- which(is.na(idx))
>     pos_key <- paste0(sub("^chr", "", as.character(chr[need]), ignore.case = TRUE), "_", pos[need])
>     pidx <- match(pos_key, intro$pos_key)
>     map_pair <- intro$alleles[pidx]
>     ok <- !is.na(pidx) & (is.na(map_pair) |
>                           map_pair == allele_pair(a1[need], a2[need]) |
>                           map_pair == allele_pair(complement(a1[need]), complement(a2[need])))
>     ok <- ok %in% TRUE                                  # NA (e.g. missing GWAS allele) -> no match
>     idx[need[ok]] <- pidx[ok]
>   }
>   idx
> }
> annotate_introgressed <- function(variants, intro, use_position) {
>   idx <- variants[, match_introgressed(rsID, chr, pos, gwas_ea, gwas_oa, intro, use_position)]
>   variants[, `:=`(
>     is_neanderthal     = !is.na(idx),
>     introgression_maps = intro$maps[idx],
>     neanderthal_allele = intro$neanderthal_allele[idx],
>     notes              = intro$notes[idx]
>   )]
>   variants[, neanderthal_beta := NA_real_]
>   known <- variants[, !is.na(neanderthal_allele)]
>   variants[known, neanderthal_beta := fcase(
>     neanderthal_allele == ref_A1, beta,
>     neanderthal_allele == ref_A2, -beta,
>     !palindromic & complement(neanderthal_allele) == ref_A1, beta,
>     !palindromic & complement(neanderthal_allele) == ref_A2, -beta,
>     default = NA_real_
>   )]
>   variants[!is.na(neanderthal_allele) & is.na(neanderthal_beta),
>            notes := "Neanderthal allele matches neither GWAS allele"]
>   invisible(variants)
> }
> run_plink <- function(args) {
>   cmd <- glue("{PLINK_MODULE}; plink {args}")
>   status <- system(cmd)
>   if (status != 0) stop(glue("PLINK failed (exit status {status}):\n{cmd}"))
>   invisible(status)
> }
> compute_ld <- function(rsids, chr, ancestry_group, out_prefix) {
>   ld_ref <- file.path(LD_PANEL_DIR, ancestry_group, glue("1000G_{ancestry_group}_chr{chr}"))
>   rsid_file <- glue("{out_prefix}_variants.txt")
>   writeLines(rsids, rsid_file)
> 
>   message(glue("Running PLINK for chr{chr}..."))
>   # --mac 1 drops variants monomorphic in this ancestry group and keeps singletons.
>   # Equivalent to MAF >= 1/(2N) for any panel size N, without floating-point edge cases.
>   n_ref <- nrow(fread(glue("{ld_ref}.fam"), header = FALSE))
>   message(glue("LD panel {ancestry_group}: N = {n_ref}; min MAF = 1/(2N) = {signif(1 / (2 * n_ref), 3)}"))
>   run_plink(glue("--bfile {ld_ref} --extract {rsid_file} --mac 1 ",
>                  "--keep-allele-order --make-bed --out {out_prefix}"))
> 
>   # --keep-allele-order is required here too: without it PLINK 1.9 swaps A2 to
>   # the major allele before --r, so LD signs would not match the .bim A1 used
>   # to align betas
>   run_plink(glue("--bfile {out_prefix} --keep-allele-order --r square --out {out_prefix}_ld"))
> 
>   bim <- fread(glue("{out_prefix}.bim"), header = FALSE,
>                col.names = c("chr", "rsID", "cm", "pos", "ref_A1", "ref_A2"),
>                colClasses = list(character = c(1, 2, 5, 6)))           # alleles as character ("T" != TRUE)
>   ld <- as.matrix(fread(glue("{out_prefix}_ld.ld"), header = FALSE))
>   dimnames(ld) <- list(bim$rsID, bim$rsID)
> 
>   list(bim = bim, ld = ld, n_ref = n_ref)
> }
> complement <- function(alleles) chartr("ATCG", "TAGC", alleles)
> align_alleles <- function(window_variants, bim, drop_palindromic = TRUE) {
>   aligned <- merge(bim[, .(rsID, ref_A1, ref_A2)], window_variants, by = "rsID", sort = FALSE)
>   allele_cols <- c("gwas_ea", "gwas_oa", "ref_A1", "ref_A2")
>   aligned[, (allele_cols) := lapply(.SD, toupper), .SDcols = allele_cols]
>   aligned[, palindromic := paste0(ref_A1, ref_A2) %in% PALINDROMIC_PAIRS]
> 
>   n_palindromic <- 0L
>   if (drop_palindromic) {
>     n_palindromic <- sum(aligned$palindromic)
>     if (n_palindromic > 0) message(glue("Dropping {n_palindromic} strand-ambiguous (A/T, C/G) variants."))
>     aligned <- aligned[palindromic == FALSE]
>   }
> 
>   # Direct matches take priority; complement (strand) matching only for
>   # non-palindromic variants, where it is unambiguous
>   aligned[, `:=`(
>     match_direct = gwas_ea == ref_A1 & gwas_oa == ref_A2,
>     flip_direct  = gwas_ea == ref_A2 & gwas_oa == ref_A1,
>     match_comp   = !palindromic & complement(gwas_ea) == ref_A1 & complement(gwas_oa) == ref_A2,
>     flip_comp    = !palindromic & complement(gwas_ea) == ref_A2 & complement(gwas_oa) == ref_A1
>   )]
>   aligned[, keep_orient := match_direct | (!flip_direct & match_comp)]
>   aligned[, do_flip := !keep_orient & (flip_direct | flip_comp)]
> 
>   n_matched   <- sum(aligned$keep_orient)
>   n_flipped   <- sum(aligned$do_flip)
>   n_unmatched <- sum(!(aligned$keep_orient | aligned$do_flip))
>   message(glue("Allele alignment: {n_matched} matched, {n_flipped} flipped, {n_unmatched} dropped."))
> 
>   aligned[do_flip == TRUE, beta := -beta]
>   aligned <- aligned[keep_orient | do_flip]
>   aligned[, c("match_direct", "flip_direct", "match_comp", "flip_comp", "keep_orient", "do_flip") := NULL]
> 
>   list(variants = aligned, n_palindromic = n_palindromic, n_unmatched = n_unmatched)
> }
> prepare_ld_matrix <- function(ld_full, rsids, lambda_shrink = 0) {
>   ld <- ld_full[rsids, rsids, drop = FALSE]
>   ld[is.na(ld)] <- 0
>   ld <- (ld + t(ld)) / 2
>   diag(ld) <- diag(ld) + 1e-4
>   ld <- stats::cov2cor(ld)
> 
>   if (lambda_shrink > 0) {
>     message(glue("Applying {lambda_shrink * 100}% LD shrinkage toward the identity."))
>     ld <- (1 - lambda_shrink) * ld + lambda_shrink * diag(nrow(ld))
>   }
>   ld
> }
> run_kriging <- function(z_scores, ld, n_samples, variants) {
>   message("Running consistency diagnostic (Kriging)...")
>   kriging <- susieR::kriging_rss(z = z_scores, R = ld, n = n_samples)
>   cd <- kriging$conditional_dist
> 
>   # susieR vignette: flag logLR > 2 & |z| > 2. logLR > 10 reported as severe.
>   flagged <- which(cd$logLR > 2 & abs(cd$z) > 2)
>   n_severe <- sum(cd$logLR > 10)
> 
>   flag_table <- data.table(
>     rsID           = variants$rsID[flagged],
>     pos            = variants$pos[flagged],
>     z_score        = cd$z[flagged],
>     log_lr         = cd$logLR[flagged],
>     is_neanderthal = variants$is_neanderthal[flagged]
>   )[order(-log_lr)]
> 
>   if (nrow(flag_table) > 0) {
>     message(glue("{nrow(flag_table)} SNPs flagged (logLR > 2 & |z| > 2); {n_severe} with logLR > 10:"))
>     print(flag_table)
>   } else {
>     message("Kriging: 0 SNPs flagged (logLR > 2 & |z| > 2).")
>   }
> 
>   list(result = kriging, flagged = flag_table, n_severe = n_severe)
> }
> summarize_credible_sets <- function(fitted, cs_info, variants, z_scores,
>                                     window_start, window_end, edge_buffer_bp = 1e5) {
>   if (is.null(cs_info$cs)) return(list(cs_table = NULL, cs_summary = NULL))
> 
>   is_nea <- variants$is_neanderthal
>   cs_names <- names(cs_info$cs)
>   effect_idx <- as.integer(sub("L", "", cs_names))
> 
>   cs_table <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_along(cs_info$cs), function(k) {
>     idx <- cs_info$cs[[k]]
>     data.table(
>       CS                 = cs_names[k],
>       rsID               = variants$rsID[idx],
>       pos                = variants$pos[idx],
>       effect_allele      = variants$ref_A1[idx],   # beta is oriented to this allele after alignment
>       other_allele       = variants$ref_A2[idx],
>       PIP                = fitted$pip[idx],
>       alpha              = fitted$alpha[effect_idx[k], idx],
>       beta               = variants$beta[idx],
>       Z                  = z_scores[idx],
>       purity             = cs_info$purity[k, "min.abs.corr"],
>       is_neanderthal     = is_nea[idx],
>       introgression_maps = variants$introgression_maps[idx],
>       neanderthal_allele = variants$neanderthal_allele[idx],
>       neanderthal_beta   = variants$neanderthal_beta[idx],
>       notes              = variants$notes[idx]
>     )
>   }))
> 
>   # p_neanderthal: posterior probability that the causal variant for this effect
>   # is a Neanderthal allele (sum of this effect's alpha over Neanderthal variants)
>   cs_summary <- data.table(
>     CS             = cs_names,
>     n_variants     = lengths(cs_info$cs),
>     n_neanderthal  = sapply(cs_info$cs, function(idx) sum(is_nea[idx])),
>     p_neanderthal  = rowSums(fitted$alpha[effect_idx, is_nea, drop = FALSE]),
>     max_pip        = sapply(cs_info$cs, function(idx) max(fitted$pip[idx])),
>     max_abs_z      = sapply(cs_info$cs, function(idx) max(abs(z_scores[idx]))),
>     purity         = cs_info$purity[, "min.abs.corr"],
>     prior_variance = fitted$V[effect_idx],
>     near_window_edge = sapply(cs_info$cs, function(idx) {
>       any(variants$pos[idx] < window_start + edge_buffer_bp |
>           variants$pos[idx] > window_end - edge_buffer_bp)
>     })
>   )
> 
>   cs_table <- cs_summary[, .(CS, p_neanderthal)][cs_table, on = "CS"]
>   list(cs_table = cs_table[order(CS, -PIP)], cs_summary = cs_summary)
> }
> fine_mapping <- function(introgressed,                    # from load_introgressed_variants()
>                          config_key,
>                          ancestry_group,
>                          locus_id,
>                          n_samples,
>                          lead_rsid,
>                          window_size = 1000,               # total window in kb (1000 = +/-500 kb)
>                          L = 10,
>                          max_iter = 1000,
>                          min_lambda = 0.01,
>                          estimate_prior_variance = TRUE,
>                          refine = FALSE,
>                          lambda_shrink = 0,
>                          drop_variants = NULL,
>                          drop_palindromic = TRUE,
>                          keep_plink_files = FALSE,
>                          save_results = TRUE,
>                          main_file = MAIN_FILE,           # NULL to skip appending
>                          sumstats = NULL) {               # optional pre-loaded sumstats (faster for many loci)
> 
>   # PLINK intermediates (.bed/.bim/.fam/.ld/.log/variant list) go to a per-run
>   # temp directory and are deleted on exit. Set keep_plink_files = TRUE to keep
>   # them under FM_DIR/plink/<config_key>/ for debugging.
>   run_name <- glue("{config_key}_{locus_id}_{ancestry_group}_1KG_filtered")
>   if (keep_plink_files) {
>     plink_dir <- file.path(FM_DIR, "plink", config_key)
>   } else {
>     plink_dir <- tempfile(pattern = paste0(run_name, "_"))
>     on.exit(unlink(plink_dir, recursive = TRUE), add = TRUE)
>   }
>   dir.create(plink_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
>   out_prefix <- file.path(plink_dir, run_name)
> 
>   # --- LOAD AND WINDOW ---
>   sumstats_provided <- !is.null(sumstats)
>   config <- load_gwas_config(config_key, quiet = sumstats_provided)
>   if (!sumstats_provided) sumstats <- load_sumstats(config)
> 
>   # Introgression maps are hg19; match by position only when GWAS positions are hg19 too
>   use_position <- identical(config$positions_build, "hg19")
>   if (!use_position) {
>     warning(glue("{config_key}: GWAS positions are on '{config$positions_build}', not hg19. ",
>                  "Matching introgressed variants by rsID only."))
>   }
>   count_nea <- function(dt) {
>     sum(!is.na(match_introgressed(dt$rsID, dt$chr, dt$pos, dt$gwas_ea, dt$gwas_oa, introgressed, use_position)))
>   }
>   # Genome-wide count is slow on a full GWAS; run_all_loci reports it once per GWAS instead
>   n_nea_in_gwas <- NA_integer_
>   if (!sumstats_provided) {
>     n_nea_in_gwas <- count_nea(sumstats)
>     message(glue("Introgressed variants found in GWAS: {n_nea_in_gwas} of {nrow(introgressed)} ",
>                  "({round(100 * n_nea_in_gwas / nrow(introgressed), 1)}%)."))
>   }
>   locus    <- extract_window(sumstats, lead_rsid, window_size, drop_variants)
>   rm(sumstats)
> 
>   # --- LD REFERENCE ---
>   ld_panel <- compute_ld(locus$variants$rsID, locus$chr, ancestry_group, out_prefix)
> 
>   # --- ALLELE ALIGNMENT ---
>   alignment <- align_alleles(locus$variants, ld_panel$bim, drop_palindromic)
>   variants  <- alignment$variants
>   ld_mat    <- prepare_ld_matrix(ld_panel$ld, variants$rsID, lambda_shrink)
>   z_scores  <- variants$beta / variants$se
>   annotate_introgressed(variants, introgressed, use_position)
> 
>   attrition <- list(in_gwas     = n_nea_in_gwas,
>                     window      = count_nea(locus$variants),
>                     in_ld_panel = count_nea(locus$variants[rsID %in% ld_panel$bim$rsID]),
>                     aligned     = sum(variants$is_neanderthal))
> 
>   # --- DIAGNOSTICS ---
>   kriging <- run_kriging(z_scores, ld_mat, n_samples, variants)
> 
>   # --- SUSIE ---
>   message("Executing susie_rss...")
>   fitted <- susie_rss(
>     bhat = variants$beta,
>     shat = variants$se,
>     R    = ld_mat,
>     n    = n_samples,
>     L    = L,
>     max_iter = max_iter,
>     min_lambda = min_lambda,
>     estimate_prior_variance = estimate_prior_variance,
>     refine = refine,
>     check_ridge = TRUE,
>     verbose = FALSE,
>     tol = 1e-3
>   )
>   if (!isTRUE(fitted$converged)) warning(glue("susie_rss did not converge for {locus_id} ({config_key})."))
>   message(glue("Model ELBO for L = {L}: {round(tail(fitted$elbo, 1), 2)}"))
> 
>   # --- CREDIBLE SETS ---
>   cs_info <- susie_get_cs(fitted, Xcorr = ld_mat)
>   cs <- summarize_credible_sets(fitted, cs_info, variants, z_scores,
>                                 locus$start, locus$end)
> 
>   if (is.null(cs$cs_summary)) {
>     message("No credible sets detected.")
>   } else {
>     message(glue("Found {nrow(cs$cs_summary)} credible sets."))
>     print(cs$cs_summary)
>     print(cs$cs_table)
>     sign_check <- cs$cs_table[!is.na(neanderthal_beta), .(n_signs = uniqueN(sign(neanderthal_beta))), by = CS]
>     if (any(sign_check$n_signs > 1)) {
>       warning(glue("Neanderthal-allele betas change sign within a credible set at {locus_id}; check allele coding."))
>     }
>     if (any(cs$cs_summary$near_window_edge)) {
>       warning(glue("Credible set within 100 kb of the window edge for {locus_id}; rerun with a larger window_size."))
>     }
>   }
> 
>   message(glue("Neanderthal variants retained: window {attrition$window} -> ",
>                "LD panel {attrition$in_ld_panel} -> aligned {attrition$aligned}"))
> 
>   # --- OUTPUT ---
>   ids <- data.table(cancer = config_key, ancestry_group = ancestry_group,
>                     locus_id = locus_id, lead_rsid = lead_rsid, chr = locus$chr)
> 
>   locus_summary <- cbind(ids, data.table(
>     window_start      = locus$start,
>     window_end        = locus$end,
>     window_size       = window_size,
>     L                 = L,
>     n_variants        = nrow(variants),
>     n_neanderthal     = attrition$aligned,
>     n_credible_sets   = if (is.null(cs$cs_summary)) 0L else nrow(cs$cs_summary),
>     n_neanderthal_cs  = if (is.null(cs$cs_summary)) 0L else sum(cs$cs_summary$n_neanderthal > 0),
>     converged         = isTRUE(fitted$converged),
>     elbo              = tail(fitted$elbo, 1),
>     n_kriging_flagged = nrow(kriging$flagged),
>     n_kriging_severe  = kriging$n_severe
>   ))
> 
>   if (!is.null(cs$cs_summary)) {
>     cs$cs_summary <- cbind(ids, cs$cs_summary)
>     cs$cs_table   <- cbind(ids, cs$cs_table)
>   }
> 
>   variant_table <- variants[, .(rsID, chr, pos, effect_allele = ref_A1, other_allele = ref_A2, beta, se)]
>   variant_table[, `:=`(Z = z_scores, PIP = fitted$pip)]
>   variant_table <- cbind(variant_table, variants[, .(is_neanderthal, introgression_maps, neanderthal_allele,
>                                                      neanderthal_beta, notes)])
> 
>   result <- list(
>     locus_summary         = locus_summary,
>     model                 = fitted,
>     variants              = variant_table,
>     cs                    = cs_info$cs,
>     cs_table              = cs$cs_table,
>     cs_summary            = cs$cs_summary,
>     pip                   = fitted$pip,
>     ld                    = ld_mat,
>     kriging               = kriging$result,
>     kriging_flagged       = kriging$flagged,
>     converged             = isTRUE(fitted$converged),
>     neanderthal_attrition = attrition,
>     settings              = list(window_size = window_size, L = L,
>                                  estimate_prior_variance = estimate_prior_variance,
>                                  refine = refine,
>                                  lambda_shrink = lambda_shrink,
>                                  drop_palindromic = drop_palindromic,
>                                  drop_variants = drop_variants,
>                                  n_ld_panel = ld_panel$n_ref)
>   )
> 
>   if (save_results) save_locus_result(result)
>   if (!is.null(main_file)) append_to_main_file(result, main_file)
>   invisible(result)
> }

The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

The scripts that did not run through read 6 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `agvs_hg38.txt.gz`, `aadr_sample_annotation_basic.txt.gz`, `addsnps2haploldpopulations.pkl`, `addsnps2onekg.pkl`, `addsnps2altai.pkl`, `addsnps2afinafr.pkl`.
#### Parsing
1 Python file is written for Python 2, which has been unsupported since 2020. We ran it with Python 2.7 (Docker image `python:2.7-slim`), with the last versions of its packages that support Python 2, which can differ from the versions the authors used. We did not convert the code. Python 2 gets no more fixes, so the authors could convert it to Python 3: mtdna_uncompress_v66.p1.py.
#### Execution
**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 24 scripts: 1 ran without error, 7 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 1 file was not run on its own, because other files import it: utils.py (by analysis.ipynb). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). 1 script is written for Python 2, so it was run with Python 2.7 instead of Python 3: mtdna_uncompress_v66.p1.py.

text.text: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals.
Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer.
However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated.
Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry.
Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk.
Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal (≥ 50% posterior inclusion probability).
Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk.

Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy.
Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry.
As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers.
However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data.
These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against.
However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects.
This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.

The genomes of modern humans reflect complex demography and migration patterns over the past hundreds of thousands of years, including interbreeding with other hominin lineages, such as Neanderthals (Green et al., 2010; Nielsen et al., 2017).

text.text: Although Neanderthal DNA remains largely in genomic regions under low evolutionarily constraint, Neanderthal alleles are associated with many traits in various biological domains (Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; McArthur, Rinker, and Capra, 2021; Simonti et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2023).

text.text: Neanderthal ancestry has been proposed to promote somatic mutations in liver cancer (Taravella Oill, Buetow, and Wilson, 2022), but the contribution of Neanderthal variants to germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated.

text.text: Here, we quantify the contribution of Neanderthal variants to cancer risk by integrating GWAS for 17 cancers with Neanderthal ancestry maps.
First, we identify cancers whose significantly associated loci harbor Neanderthal alleles.
Second, we conduct fine-mapping to nominate putatively causal Neanderthal variants.
Third, we highlight multiple fine-mapped example variants, including Neanderthal alleles that influence breast cancer and skin cancer risk but have positively selected pleiotropic effects.
Finally, we quantify enrichment for heritability of cancer risk among regions of Neanderthal ancestry using summary statistics and replicate our results using individual-level genotype data.

We identified autosomal Neanderthal ancestry variants based on four previous maps of Neanderthal introgression with single-nucleotide variant (SNV) resolution: Browning et al. 2018 , Sankararaman et al. 2016 , Skov 2024 , and Vernot et al. 2016.

text.text: As expected, the number of potential Neanderthal associations is sensitive to the LD threshold used to define a locus (Fig. S3, Table S3).

text.text: Many GWAS typically use a permissive LD threshold, such as r 2 > 0.2.
text.formatted: Many GWAS typically use a permissive LD threshold, such as r 2 > 0.2.

text.text: This approach yields higher proportions of loci with Neanderthal variants but fewer loci overall.
A stricter LD threshold of r² = 0.8 results in lower proportions of loci with Neanderthal variants, but more cancer-associated loci overall.
Therefore, we chose r² = 0.5 for downstream analyses to balance the tradeoff between loci containing Neanderthal variants and overall number of independent loci.
The co-localization of germline cancer risk variants and Neanderthal variants could reflect causal roles for the Neanderthal alleles.

However, it is also possible that the Neanderthal variants are simply in high LD with causal variants that mutated onto Neanderthal haplotypes after introgression (Rinker et al., 2020; Skov et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, it is also possible that the Neanderthal variants are simply in high LD with causal variants that mutated onto Neanderthal haplotypes after introgression <ref type="bibr">(Rinker et al., 2020; Skov et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: To resolve these scenarios, we used statistical fine-mapping to estimate whether Neanderthal variants are among the credible sets for causally influencing germline cancer risk.
First, we identified genome-wide significant loci in each GWAS with Neanderthal variants (Fig. 3A).
text.formatted: First, we identified genome-wide significant loci in each GWAS with Neanderthal variants (Fig. <ref type="figure">3A</ref>).

text.text: Within each GWAS, we started with the most strongly associated Neanderthal variant, included all Neanderthal variants within 500 kb, and then moved on to the next most strongly associated remaining variant to define the next locus, and so on.
We then fine-mapped the ±500 kb window around each index variant with SuSiE-RSS, using ancestry-matched 1000 Genomes LD reference panels.
We fine-mapped 165 loci, of which 152 converged or were rescued by refitting (Table S4).

text.text: These comprised 448 credible sets across 148 loci, 306 of which contained a variant reaching genome-wide significance (|Z| ≥ 5.45, P < 5 × 10 -8 ) (Table S5).

text.text: In 32 of these 70 associations, the posterior probability that the causal variant is a Neanderthal variant exceeded 50% (Fig. 3B, Tables S6-7).

text.text: The 32 associations span nine GWAS and seven cancers: basal cell carcinoma, breast, colorectal, prostate, renal, squamous cell carcinoma, and testicular cancer.

Previous work has demonstrated that introgressed Neanderthal variants are associated with and enriched for effects on integumentary and pigmentation phenotypes (Vernot and Akey, 2014; Racimo et al., 2015; Simonti et al., 2016; Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; McArthur, Rinker, and Capra, 2021).

text.text: Thus, we were particularly curious whether Neanderthal variants contribute to the risk landscape for skin cancers.

Indeed, seven of the 32 Neanderthal-majority associations, across six loci, are in skin cancers: two unique to basal cell carcinoma (BCC), three unique to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and an association in the BNC2 locus, which is shared by both (Fig. 3B).

Two Neanderthal variant sets associate with multiple cancers: the KLK cluster on 19q13.33 associates with both prostate and testicular cancer, and the BNC2 locus with basal and squamous cell carcinoma.

Five of the 32 Neanderthal cancer associations intersect regions previously identified as adaptively introgressed: variants near PABPC4 for squamous cell carcinoma, BNC2 for both basal and squamous cell carcinoma, the type II keratin cluster on chromosome 12 for basal cell carcinoma, and variants within LPAR1 for colorectal cancer (Table S9).

text.text: Four more fall within 30 kb of a region with evidence of adaptive introgression: variants within RHPN2 for colorectal cancer, within RAD51B for breast cancer, and near PTHLH for breast cancer in both ancestry groups (Table S9).

text.text: We examine two of the cancer-associated loci with evidence of adaptive introgression (BNC2, PTHLH) in more detail in the following sections.
Notably, four of the five cancer-associated loci overlapping evidence of adaptive introgression function in the hair and skin.
High frequency Neanderthal variants in the BNC2 locus that are implicated in many studies of adaptive introgression associate with increased risk for both BCC and SCC (see below).
In addition, adaptively introgressed Neanderthal alleles associate with decreased risk (rs687751 β = -0.100) for BCC in the type II keratin cluster on chromosome 12.
Meanwhile, Neanderthal variants near PABPC4 on chromosome 1 associate with increased SCC risk (rs3768321 β = 0.041) (Fig. S6).

text.text: We quantified heritability enrichment for Neanderthal variants for each cancer GWAS using stratified LD score regression (S-LDSC) against the baseline model, using 1000 Genomes as the reference panel.
We considered each of the four introgression maps separately for each GWAS to better evaluate robustness of the conclusions to the introgression mapping strategy used.

Of the 28 GWAS with available effect sizes, eight carried sufficient heritability signal for partitioned analysis (mean χ2 ≥ 1.02 and an observed-scale heritability ≥ 0.05): basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, breast cancer in both ancestry groups, colorectal and lung cancer in Europeans, and prostate cancer in both ancestry groups (Fig. 7, Table S15).

text.text: The remaining 20 were excluded for failure to meet one or both criteria.

Given the breast cancer risk heritability enrichment among Neanderthal variants in published GWAS, we validated this signal using individual-level genotypes from the UK Biobank, which contributes to neither breast cancer GWAS analysed here.

In a cohort of 14,346 cases and 40,126 matched controls, Neanderthal variants were enriched for breast cancer heritability across all four introgression maps, ranging from 1.22 to 14.85x, although no individual estimate was statistically significant (Pazokitoroudi et al., 2024; Fig. 7C).

text.text: These results suggest that Neanderthal variants are not enriched for contributions to risk of most cancers, but that they may contribute more than expected to breast cancer risk.

Despite the relatively small number of loci containing high-confidence fine-mapped Neanderthal variants, the observed enrichments provide complementary evidence that Neanderthal introgressed regions contribute to cancer risk beyond the genome-wide significant loci captured in the fine-mapping analysis.

Interbreeding between Neanderthals and humans emigrating from Africa ∼47,000 years ago has left a complex phenotypic legacy among modern humans (Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; Simonti et al., 2016; McArthur, Rinker, and Capra, 2021; Wei et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Interbreeding between Neanderthals and humans emigrating from Africa ∼47,000 years ago has left a complex phenotypic legacy among modern humans <ref type="bibr">(Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; Simonti et al., 2016; McArthur, Rinker, and Capra, 2021; Wei et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Given the effects of Neanderthal ancestry on immune and metabolic processes linked to cancer risk and progression, we integrated maps of introgression and cancer GWAS data to evaluate the contribution of Neanderthal alleles to germline risk for multiple cancers.
We discovered that risk loci for multiple cancers in both European and East Asian ancestry groups harbor Neanderthal alleles.
Fine-mapping revealed 32 associations likely caused by Neanderthal variants.
Given the small contribution of common germline variants to risk for most cancers, the Neanderthal associations may be somewhat surprising.

Our analyses reveal several insights that 14 Prostate Breast 0.25 0.50 1.00 2.00 4.00 Heritability Enrichment in Neanderthal Variants Cancer East Asian GWAS A BCC Prostate Lung SCC Colorectal Breast 0.25 0.50 1.00 2.00 4.00 Heritability Enrichment in Neanderthal Variants Cancer European GWAS B Breast 0.25 0.5 1 2 4 8 16 Heritability Enrichment in Neanderthal Variants Cancer UK Biobankindividual-level genotypes C Enrichment Neither Enriched or Depleted Depletion 15 help explain the presence of associations between Neanderthal variants and cancer.
First, while 14 of the significantly cancer-associated Neanderthal variants increase risk, 18 Neanderthal variants decrease risk.
This differs from most other traits studied where Neanderthal variants mostly increase risk and many contribute to their maintenance.
Second, a substantial number of the associations we discover (9 of 32) are in regions with evidence of adaptive introgression, including BNC2 and PABPC4.
At BNC2, the Neanderthal allele is associated with lighter pigmentation as well as with increased skin cancer risk (Table S12).
text.formatted: At BNC2, the Neanderthal allele is associated with lighter pigmentation as well as with increased skin cancer risk (Table <ref type="table">S12</ref>).

text.text: Pigmentation levels govern cumulative ultraviolet exposure.
This suggests a mechanism of mediated pleiotropy, in which the cancer association is a downstream consequence of the adaptive pigmentation effect rather than an independent functional effect.

Several of the other adaptive introgression loci with cancer associations include genes like PABPC4 that encode multi-functional proteins involved in viral interactions and immune response, further suggesting pleiotropic mechanisms underlying the cancer associations.
Because most cancer risk is realized after reproduction, an allele favored for an earlier-life effect can carry a cancer cost that purifying selection acts on only weakly.
Finally, with the exception of breast cancer, Neanderthal variants are depleted or neutral in their contributions to nearly all tested cancers.
This is consistent with patterns seen for most non-cancer traits due to the selection against Neanderthal ancestry in many functional regions of the genome.
Several features of breast cancer may contribute to the enrichment.
Breast cancer risk depends strongly on lifetime reproductive hormone exposure and sensitivity.

Neanderthal haplotypes have been associated with reproductive phenotypes, e.g., via a change in the progesterone receptor that increases its sensitivity and increases fertility (Zeberg, Kelso, and Pääbo, 2020).
text.formatted: Neanderthal haplotypes have been associated with reproductive phenotypes, e.g., via a change in the progesterone receptor that increases its sensitivity and increases fertility <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Zeberg, Kelso, and Pääbo, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, it is possible that the enrichment reflects antagonistic pleiotropy in which variants retained for early life effects on reproductive success could contribute to increased breast cancer risk.
Similarly, breast tumors develop in an environment dominated by adipocytes (fat cells) in which lipid-induced inflammation often contributes to risk.

Neanderthal alleles have adaptive effects on lipid metabolism (Khrameeva et al., 2014) and immune activity (Abi-Rached et al., 2011; Mendez, Watkins, and Hammer, 2012; Sams et al., 2016; Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; Zhou et al., 2021; Jagoda et al., 2022; Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020; Zeberg and Pääbo, 2021).

text.text: Finally, the genetic architecture of breast cancer is highly polygenic and focused in non-coding regulatory regions, and the Neanderthal variants that persist in modern human genomes are also predominantly regulatory rather than coding (McCoy, Wakefield, and Akey, 2017).
text.formatted: Finally, the genetic architecture of breast cancer is highly polygenic and focused in non-coding regulatory regions, and the Neanderthal variants that persist in modern human genomes are also predominantly regulatory rather than coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(McCoy, Wakefield, and Akey, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: While our results provide an important first step toward understanding how introgression from Neanderthals has contributed to germline cancer risk in modern humans, we acknowledge several limitations to our approach.
First, while cancers vary in their genetic architecture and germline risk, our results are influenced by differences statistical power between the cancer GWAS considered.
The number of fine-mapped Neanderthal associations identified per GWAS correlates with statistical power.
We also note that several of the GWAS considered either used the same cohort (e.g., basal and squamous cell carcinoma) or included data from the UK Biobank.

For example, the basal and squamous cell carcinoma summary statistics are the output of a multi-trait analysis of GWAS across keratinocyte cancer phenotypes rather than single-trait association tests, so their effect estimates borrow information across those phenotypes.
Thus, the two associations we report at BNC2 may reflect a single signal.
However, we note that the breast cancer GWAS are independent.

Second, while we consider multi-16 ple introgression maps, they are ultimately incomplete and are also underpowered to detect certain classes of variants, including reintroduced ancestral alleles as exemplified by uncalled variants near PTHLH.
Therefore, the posteriors reported here are likely lower bounds on the Neanderthal contribution.
Third, the methods for identifying Neanderthal variants and for fine mapping depend on an external LD reference.

The 1000 Genomes panels used here comprise roughly 500 individuals per ancestry group, so LD involving variants too rare to be well represented cannot be estimated reliably and those variants cannot be fine-mapped.
The panel also stands in for each study cohort's own LD, and mismatch between the two is an inherent limitation of summary-statistic-based fine-mapping.

The kriging diagnostic flagged 520 variants as potentially inconsistent with the reference panel; only 12 fell within a credible set, none were Neanderthal variants, and none occurred among the Neanderthal-majority associations (Table S17), so this is unlikely to affect the associations we report.

text.text: Fourth, despite the increasing availability of genetic data from peoples of non-European ancestry (Fatumo et al., 2022), there are few publicly available cancer GWAS beyond those used in the present analysis.

text.text: As additional data become available, disentangling ancestry-group specific cancer risk and differences in Neanderthal contributions will be possible.
This will be particularly relevant given known differences in Neanderthal ancestry between continental groups (Vernot and Akey, 2014).

text.text: Further, additional data from individuals from the Americas, southern Asia, and Oceania will enable analysis of Denisovan ancestry on cancer risk, as Denisovan ancestry is highest in these populations (Vernot et al., 2016; Sankararaman et al., 2016; Browning et al., 2018).

text.text: Mapping the contribution of Neanderthal variants to modern human cancer risk adds to our understanding of phenotypic differences and similarities between these groups.
However, it also provides valuable context for interpreting the causes of cancer and the pleiotropic mechanisms sustaining cancer-associated variation.
Neanderthal variation can be dated and its selective history reconstructed, making it a tractable system for asking how early-life selection shapes the genetic architecture of late-onset disease.

text.text: Many methods have been developed to identify introgressed DNA in a target population, yet the sets of inferred introgressed variants and regions can vary substantially, even when applied to the same population (Chen, Velazquez-Arcelay, and Capra, 2026).

text.text: Therefore, we used four different Neanderthal introgression datasets that span algorithm architectures and feature variant-level calls : Browning et al., 2018 , Sankararaman et al., 2016 , Skov, 2024 , and Vernot et al., 2016. Three of the four datasets below use at least one reference genome from an archaic hominin to identify variants and groups of variants or haplotypes.

text.text: Hereafter, we refer to the latter as "regions".

The high-coverage (∼52X) Neanderthal genome used in the methods below is Denisova 5, an ∼120,000 year old specimen from a female who was recovered from the Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of southern Siberia (Prüfer et al., 2014).

text.text: We refer to this specimen as the "Altai Neanderthal".
Introgression methods may also identify Neanderthal alleles in modern humans using a second archaic hominin genome from a sister lineage to Neanderthals-Denisovans.
A high-coverage (∼31X) genome is available from Denisova 3, a 70,000 year old specimen that was also recovered from Denisova Cave (Meyer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: A high-coverage (∼31X) genome is available from Denisova 3, a 70,000 year old specimen that was also recovered from Denisova Cave <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Meyer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: We refer to this specimen as the "Denisovan".

The Browning et al. 2018 dataset was generated using Sprime-a scoring method that identifies introgressed haplotypes using an archaic reference genome, the expected length of such haplotypes, and clusters of derived alleles that are absent in an unadmixed outgroup.
Sprime further adjusts the score based on the local mutation and recombination rates, allows for low-frequency introgression in the unadmixed outgroup and avoids windowing.
To be conservative, we required that the variants in this dataset match the Altai Neanderthal (NMATCH = match).

We defined introgressed regions per the authors such that a Neanderthal region must comprise ≥ 30 variants that could be assessed in both the Denisovan and Altai Neanderthal genomes (i.e., not filtered due to quality concerns).
In addition, there must be an overall match rate ≥ 0.6 for Neanderthal alleles and ≤ 0.4 for Denisovan alleles.

When applied to the 18 non-African 1000 Genomes Project (Auton et al., 2015) subpopulations and Papuans from the Simons Genome Diversity Project or SGDP (Mallick et al., 2016), Sprime identified 258,948 variants and 1,337 regions.

We used the first of two available datasets, where haplotypes are inferred using either the Denisovan or Altai Neanderthal as reference and an African genome as the unadmixed reference.
We did not apply any quality filtering to the provided haplotypes or "regions" but required that variants had a mean posterior probability of Neanderthal origin > 0.5.

text.text: The Skov 2024 dataset was generated by applying a Hidden Markov Model to modern human sequences.
This model has two hidden states: 1) ingroup or segments of non-introgressed DNA and 2) archaic or segments of introgressed DNA.

This method leverages the density of private variants in a queried sample, such that segments of introgressed DNA will have a longer time to accumulate variants due to deeper coalescence, and thus will exhibit a higher density of private variants compared to segments of non-introgressed DNA.
This method does not require an archaic genome for comparison but does require an unadmixed outgroup (i.e., Africans).

We identified regions by filtering for segments whose mean posterior probability that a segment was archaic was ≥ 0.8 and whose likely source was either Neanderthal or both (i.e., Neanderthal and Denisovan).

We collated segments called in 1000 Genomes and Human Genome Diversity Project (Bergström et al., 2020) samples, merged intervals using bedtools (Quinlan and Hall, 2010), and used liftOver (Hinrichs et al., 2006) to change coordinates from the hg38 to hg19 human reference assembly.
text.formatted: We collated segments called in 1000 Genomes and Human Genome Diversity Project <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bergström et al., 2020)</ref> samples, merged intervals using bedtools <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Quinlan and Hall, 2010)</ref>, and used liftOver <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hinrichs et al., 2006)</ref> to change coordinates from the hg38 to hg19 human reference assembly.

text.text: We identified variants by filtering for those that were shared with at least one of the following Neanderthal genomic samples: Altai, Chagyrskaya, Forbes, Goyet, HST, LesCottes, Mez1, Mez2, Scladina, Spy, Vindija, VindijaG1.
When applied to samples from 1000 Genomes and HGDP, the HMM identified 354,656 variants and 4,459 regions.

The Vernot et al. 2016 dataset was generated using S*, which identifies candidate introgressed haplotypes based on clusters of derived variants that are absent from an unadmixed reference population and occur in high linkage disequilibrium.
Introgressed haplotypes are then identified by maximizing the sum of scores among all SNP subsets at a particular locus.
Tag SNPs are those variants that match an archaic allele and occur with at least two other tag SNPs in a 50 kb window.
Haplotypes were defined as regions encompassing ≥ 5 tag SNPs in LD within a given human population (r2 ≥ 0.8).
We collated tag SNPs called in 35 individuals from the Bismarck Archipelago as well as individuals from the East Asian, European, and South Asian 1000 Genomes superpopulations.
We merged overlapping haplotypes using bedtools (Quinlan and Hall, 2010) to be conservative when calling regions.
text.formatted: We merged overlapping haplotypes using bedtools <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Quinlan and Hall, 2010)</ref> to be conservative when calling regions.

text.text: Heterozygous Neanderthal allele calls were set to missing.
This procedure yielded 232,262 variants and 6,838 regions.
We merged the variant calls from the four datasets into a single union with one row per hg19 position, retaining any position called by at least one map (N = 1,085,232).
Where maps 19 reported different rsIDs or different allele pairs at a position, we retained the first value in map order (Browning, Sankararaman, Skov, Vernot) and recorded the disagreement.
text.formatted: Where maps 19 reported different rsIDs or different allele pairs at a position, we retained the first value in map order <ref type="bibr">(Browning, Sankararaman, Skov, Vernot)</ref> and recorded the disagreement.

text.text: Where maps reported different Neanderthal alleles at a position, or where the reported Neanderthal allele was not one of the variant's two alleles, the Neanderthal allele was set to missing.

To assess how common Neanderthal variants are in present-day populations, we retrieved allele frequencies for every variant in the union with an rsID from gnomAD v4.1.0 genomes (Chen et al., 2024), using PASS-filtered SNVs and matching variants by rsID, since gnomAD v4.1 is on GRCh38 and the introgression maps are on hg19.

text.text: We report the minor allele frequency (MAF), the frequency of the rarer allele, in the African/African American, East Asian, non-Finnish European and South Asian gnomAD groups, and used MAF > 1% as the threshold at which variants are common enough to be detectable in GWAS of these sizes (Fig. S2).

text.text: We constructed separate LD reference panels using 1000 Genomes data for East Asian (EAS) and European (EUR) samples.
We excluded the HG01783 sample from the EUR reference panel because this individual exhibits genetic affinity for both Iberian populations in Spain and Mende populations from Sierra Leone.
This resulted in 504 and 502 samples representing the EAS and EUR superpopulations, respectively.

We used bcftools, version 1.21 (Li, 2011), to subset biallelic SNVs per superpopulation using "view -m2 -M2 -v snps" and plink2, version 2.0.0-a.6.9 (Chang et al., 2015), to generate the files required for LD calculation.

text.text: We retained the first occurrence of duplicate variants.
Next, we retrieved significant variants from the summary statistics of each cancer GWAS using the standard genome-wide significance threshold (P = 5 × 10 -8 ).

Introgressed variants were identified by matching each significant GWAS variant against the union of the four introgression maps, first by rsID and then, for variants that remained unmatched, by hg19 position.
A position match was retained only when the two alleles reported by the introgression maps agreed with the GWAS effect and non-effect alleles, or when no map reported alleles at that position.
We performed LD clumping using plink, version 1.90b6.26 (Purcell et al., 2007), and ran the procedure at three r 2 thresholds: 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8.
text.formatted: We performed LD clumping using plink, version 1.90b6.26 <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Purcell et al., 2007)</ref>, and ran the procedure at three r 2 thresholds: 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8.

text.text: We set "clump-p1" and "clump-p2" to 1 because only genome-wide significant variants were included in the clumping procedure and used the default "clump-kb" value of 250.
We conducted this procedure separately on the introgressed subset and on all significant GWAS variants.
For each GWAS, we defined loci as non-singleton clumps, such that at least two significant variants occurred in LD at the specified r 2 threshold.

We calculated the proportion of GWAS loci containing introgressed variants by dividing the number of loci identified from the introgressed-variant subset by the total number of loci identified from all significant variants.
To conduct fine-mapping, we first identified loci in each GWAS centered on genome-wide significant Neanderthal variants.
We used a greedy approach by p-value, identifying the most strongly associated variant as the index variant for the first locus.
All Neanderthal variants within 500 kb were assigned to that locus.
Then, the next most strongly associated remaining variant defined the next.
We fine-mapped a ±500 kb window around each index variant with 20 SuSiE-RSS from the susieR package (Zou et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We fine-mapped a ±500 kb window around each index variant with 20 SuSiE-RSS from the susieR package <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Zou et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For each locus, we used the aforementioned ancestry-group-specific LD reference panels calculated from 1000 Genomes.
We removed variants with missing rsIDs, duplicated rsIDs, or standard errors that were missing or ≤ 0.

Variants monomorphic in the relevant reference panel were removed with PLINK's "-mac 1", which retains singletons and is equivalent to a minor allele frequency threshold of 1/(2N), where N is the number of individuals in that ancestry group in 1000 Genomes.
Strand-ambiguous variants (A/T and C/G) were excluded before alignment.
Variants were aligned to the corresponding LD reference panel by effect and non-effect alleles, including reverse-complement strand matching, and effect estimates were sign-flipped when necessary.
Variants with irreconcilable allele mismatches were excluded.
GWAS effect estimates and standard errors were used to calculate Z-scores as Z = β/SE.

PLINK was run with "-keep-allele-order" both when extracting the panel and when computing correlations, so that the signs of the LD estimates correspond to the A1 alleles recorded in the .bim file used to align effect estimates.
The LD matrix was calculated as pairwise Pearson correlations among variants in the ancestry-specific reference panel.

Missing correlations were set to zero, the matrix was symmetrised, 10 -4 was added to the diagonal for numerical regularization and to ensure the matrix was positive definite, and the result was converted back to a correlation matrix.
We assessed consistency between the GWAS summary statistics and the ancestry-specific LD reference in the initial fits using the kriging RSS diagnostic implemented in susieR.
Variants with log LR > 2 and |z| > 2 were flagged as potentially inconsistent with the LD reference (Table S17).
text.formatted: Variants with log LR > 2 and |z| > 2 were flagged as potentially inconsistent with the LD reference (Table <ref type="table">S17</ref>).

text.text: We identified 520 variants across 115 loci, of which one exceeded the severe threshold of log LR > 10; that variant belongs to no credible set.
text.formatted: We identified 520 variants across 115 loci, of which one exceeded the severe threshold of log LR > 10; that variant belongs to no credible set.

text.text: Twelve of the 520 fell within a credible set; none is a Neanderthal variant, none belongs to a genome-wide significant credible set, and none falls within any of the 32 Neanderthal-majority associations.
We set the GWAS sample size as the effective sample size, defined as
We used a maximum of 1,000 iterations, an L = 10, a minimum λ of 0.01, and a convergence tolerance of 10 -3 .
The residual variance was estimated using the susie_rss default.
We allowed the prior variance of each single-effect component to be estimated from the data.
We initially did not perform model refinement.
Credible sets were constructed using the default 95% coverage and a purity (minimum absolute correlation among variants within each credible set) of 0.5.
For each locus we retained the original fit if it converged; otherwise a refined refit that converged, preferring L = 5 over L = 10.
Loci with no converged fit were considered unresolved.

A locus whose refit disagreed with the original about which genome-wide significant variants carried the signal (Jaccard < 0.3; one locus, at 0.25) was also treated as unresolved, since convergence to an answer that depends on initialization is not a resolved locus.
text.formatted: A locus whose refit disagreed with the original about which genome-wide significant variants carried the signal (Jaccard < 0.3; one locus, at 0.25) was also treated as unresolved, since convergence to an answer that depends on initialization is not a resolved locus.

text.text: After fine-mapping, we filtered for credible sets that contained at least one variant reaching genome-wide significance (|Z| ≥ 5.45, P = 5 × 10 -8 ).
We merged credible sets from different index windows within the same GWAS when they shared at least half their variants (Jaccard ≥ 0.5).
Next, we annotated whether or not credible set variants were Neanderthal by presence in the merged union of the four introgression maps.

Finally, we calculated the posterior probability that the causal variant is Neanderthal by summing the posterior inclusion probability of every Neanderthal variant in the fine-mapped window, not only those within the credible set.
We 21 designated Neanderthal-majority associations as those where Neanderthal posterior probability was > 50%.
text.formatted: We 21 designated Neanderthal-majority associations as those where Neanderthal posterior probability was > 50%.

text.text: We assigned a direction of effect to each Neanderthal-majority association.

For each Neanderthal variant we oriented the GWAS effect size to the Neanderthal allele, taking β as reported when the Neanderthal allele was the effect allele and -β when it was the non-effect allele.
Three of the four introgression maps report a Neanderthal allele; the Sankararaman et al. 2016 conditional random field infers Neanderthal ancestry at a SNV without naming an allele.
For variants called only by that map, we took the Neanderthal allele to be the derived allele, determined from the Ensembl human ancestor sequence (GRCh37, EPO alignment; Herrero et al., 2016).
text.formatted: For variants called only by that map, we took the Neanderthal allele to be the derived allele, determined from the Ensembl human ancestor sequence (GRCh37, EPO alignment; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Herrero et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Reintroduced ancestral alleles were excluded from this assumption, since at those sites the Neanderthal allele is ancestral by definition.
Each association was then assigned the direction carrying the greater summed posterior inclusion probability across its Neanderthal variants.
We performed conditional analysis at the PTHLH locus.
We conditioned both the East Asian and European breast cancer windows at this locus on the strongest association signal in the European GWAS: rs7297051.
Z-scores were computed as z cond = (z -rz lead )/ √ 1 -r 2 .
We defined the attenuation ratio as the conditional |Z| divided by the marginal |Z| for the credible set's lead variant (highest PIP).

To assess power, we rescaled the East Asian Z scores by the ratio of Z per unit effect size at rs788464 (a variant in both credible sets) between the two GWAS, and recomputed the conditional statistic holding r, the correlation with rs7297051 in the matched reference panel, fixed.

To assess whether structural variants (SVs) might mediate the Neanderthal-associated signals at BNC2 and PTHLH, we queried the SVatalog database (Chirmade et al., 2026), which provides LD estimates between SNPs and structural variants from 1000 Genomes long-read sequencing data.

We additionally queried gnomAD-SV v4 (Collins et al., 2020) for common structural variants (AF > 0.01) within 250 kb of the Neanderthal credible set variants for both loci.

text.text: At the PTHLH locus, we further examined 578 phased haplotypes from long-read genome assemblies spanning chr12:27,700,000-28,100,000 (hg19).

Haplotype sequences were classified by total interval size relative to the T2T reference; insertion breakpoints were localized using k-mer anchoring, and hallmarks of retrotransposition (poly-A tail, target site duplication) were assessed from the extracted insertion sequence.
We leveraged multiple datasets to assess functional effects of fine-mapped variants.

To label each Neanderthal-majority association with a gene, we used protein-coding and lncRNA genes from GENCODE v50 (basic set, GRCh37 mapping) and assigned the gene whose body is closest to the credible set's highest-PIP variant, with a distance of zero when the variant falls within the gene.

text.text: We first queried the GTEx Portal (GTEx v10) (The GTEx Consortium, 2020) for expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and splicing QTLs (sQTLs) among the credible set variants at each of the three example loci (BNC2, SLC24A4 and PTHLH).
None of the BNC2 credible set variants is a significant eQTL or sQTL in any tissue.
For loci with significant associations, we retrieved eQTL results through the GTEx Portal API for rs788464 and rs10843134 at PTHLH and rs79342051 at SLC24A4.

For each variant, we retrieved every gene-tissue pair in which it is a significant single-tissue eQTL, as defined by GTEx, together with the normalized effect size (NES), its P-value and per-sample normalized expression by genotype.
For selected genes (PTHLH, CCDC91, ENSG00000247934 and SLC24A4), we also retrieved each variant's effect in every tissue, whether or not it was significant.

GTEx reports effects for the alternate allele; we oriented all effects and genotypes to the allele of interest at each variant (the Neanderthal allele, or the reintroduced ancestral allele at rs788464).
Standard errors were computed as NES divided by the reported t statistic.
Colocalization was not tested.

To identify other phenotypes associated with the Neanderthal haplotypes at BNC2 and SLC24A4, we queried Open Targets Platform (Buniello et al., 2025) for every variant in our cancer credible sets at these loci (Tables S8 and S12), after converting positions from hg19 to GRCh38 using liftOver (Hinrichs et al., 2006).

text.text: We retained all Open Targets credible sets containing at least one of these variants and recorded the posterior probability of the query variant, along with each credible set's study, reported and mapped trait, lead variant, lead-variant effect size and P-value, fine-mapping method and top locus-to-gene (L2G) prediction.
Because Open Targets reports effect sizes for the alternate allele of each credible set's lead variant, we oriented these effects to the Neanderthal haplotype.
Lead variants present in our cancer credible sets were oriented by comparing the sign of their cancer effect with that of the Neanderthal allele.

For the remaining lead variants, we determined which allele is inherited with the Neanderthal allele of rs2026805 (BNC2) using the LDproxy tool from LDlink (Machiela and Chanock, 2015) in the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 European (EUR) panel.

We therefore used AncientProxy (Brand and Capra, 2026) to identify rs2026804 as a proxy (r² = 0.972 in TOPMed Europeans) and obtained its genotype calls for the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (AADR) v54.1.p1 from the same resource.

text.text: The allele counted is the C allele at rs2026804, which is the Neanderthal allele reported by Skov, 2024 and the derived allele relative to the human-chimpanzee ancestor.
Archaic hominin genotypes were excluded, so all frequencies reported are among modern humans.
Where a specimen was represented by more than one library, a single genotype was retained, preferring diploid shotgun calls.
These are the only source in this dataset able to call a heterozygote: every heterozygous call comes from a diploid shotgun library and no other source produces one.
The remaining sources are pseudo-haploid, reporting a true heterozygote as one homozygote or the other, and each therefore contributes a single allele rather than two.

text.text: The East Asian colorectal cancer GWAS was excluded because its summary statistics report no effect sizes, leaving 28 studies.
Summary statistics were formatted against the ancestry-matched HapMap3 variant list.
For each introgression map and ancestry group we generated annotation files and LD scores from the ancestry-matched 1000 Genomes PLINK filesets.

Each map was then modelled separately as a single annotation added to the ancestry-matched baselineLD v2.2 model (Gazal et al., 2017), with ancestry-matched regression weights and 1000 Genomes allele frequencies, giving 28 × 4 estimates.

text.text: Heritability is reported on the observed scale, since population prevalences were not available for these studies; observed-scale estimates depend on each study's case fraction and are not comparable between cancers.

The basal and squamous cell carcinoma summary statistics were genomic-control corrected by their authors (λ = 1.286 and 1.172), which deflates their reported intercepts and heritabilities, and are MTAG rather than single-trait output; enrichment is a ratio of proportions and is less sensitive to both, though MTAG test statistics are not those of a single-trait GWAS.
Several studies include UK Biobank participants and are therefore not fully independent, though neither breast cancer GWAS does.
Enrichments were interpreted only for GWAS with enough genome-wide signal to support them: mean χ2 ≥ 1.02 and an observed-scale heritability ≥ 0.05 (Tables S11-24 12).
text.formatted: Enrichments were interpreted only for GWAS with enough genome-wide signal to support them: mean χ2 ≥ 1.02 and an observed-scale heritability ≥ 0.05 (Tables <ref type="table">S11-24</ref> 12).

text.text: Enrichment P-values were corrected for multiple testing across the 32 tests conducted among the GWAS passing heritability QC (eight GWAS × four introgression maps) using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

We also estimated heritability enrichment for breast cancer from individual-level genotypes in the UK Biobank (application 226956) using GENIE v1.2.1 under an additive genetic model without an environment interaction term (Pazokitoroudi et al., 2024).

text.text: Cases were the 14,346 individuals with a breast cancer diagnosis (ICD-10 code C50) in data field 40006.

Controls were individuals with no cancer diagnosis recorded in that field; we selected three per case with nearest-neighbor matching in MatchIt (Ho et al., 2011) on sex, age, Townsend Deprivation Index and the top 20 genetic ancestry principal components, and these 23 variables were also included as fixed-effect covariates.

text.text: In contrast to the LDSC analysis, the four Neanderthal introgression maps were modelled jointly, as four annotations (4,933, 14,120, 5,844 and 2,965 variants for the Browning, Sankararaman, Skov and Vernot maps, respectively) alongside a fifth annotation comprising the remaining 516,376 variants.
Because the maps overlap, we report GENIE's overlapping-annotation enrichment estimates.
Standard errors were estimated from 100 jackknife blocks.
Total observed-scale heritability was 0.034 (SE 0.005).

All reported p-values are two-tailed, unless noted otherwise.

section.header: Characterizing germline cancer risk in the context of Neanderthal ancestry.
Loci associated with germline cancer risk harbor Neanderthal variants.
Fine-mapping nominates Neanderthal alleles as causal cancer-risk variants.
Many causal cancer-associated Neanderthal loci have evidence of adaptive introgression.
A Neanderthal haplotype at PTHLH associates with reduced breast cancer risk in both East Asians and Europeans.
